description: This is our second time participating on NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are going to do our best to solve the challenge the best way possible.
summary: NovaCare is an offline, onboard medical and psychological assistant that helps astronauts detect health problems early and act without waiting for Earth. From Mars, a message takes up to 20 minutes one way, so a question and its answer can take up to 40 minutes. NovaCare closes that gap. It learns each crew member’s personal baseline instead of using population averages, and cross-checks what astronauts report with what their data shows, so hidden fatigue, stress or pain is flagged even when someone says “I feel fine.” Every new reading is analyzed instantly on board and classified as Nominal, Watch, Needs attention or Critical, so the crew knows right away who is at risk and what to do. The working prototype at novacare.earth has five sections: Home, My Health, Crew, Mission and Insights. It includes one-minute daily check-ins, crew-wide risk analysis, medical and psychological guidance, an emergency button that works without logging in, and an offline assistant that answers from 205 protocols based on NASA-STD-3001 and Human Research Program risks. Each indicator is linked to real NASA research through an offline snapshot of the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). NovaCare adapts to five mission profiles, from a space station in low Earth orbit to a Mars base, and is designed from day one for places on Earth where a doctor is not always nearby: rural clinics, nursing homes, schools, workplaces, homes and remote sites such as Antarctic stations, ships and disaster zones.
details:
Long-duration missions expose astronauts to what NASA calls the five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile, closed environments. Together they affect the immune system, bone density, cardiovascular function and psychological well-being.

Doctors on Earth provide instructions, examinations and preventive routines, but in flight astronauts are largely responsible for monitoring their own health while also doing their jobs. As missions go farther, communication delays make immediate medical help from Earth impossible.

NovaCare is our answer: medical monitoring and management software that lets astronauts manage their health independently. It collects, stores, analyzes and compares vital signs, examination results, daily routines and behavioral patterns. By comparing what astronauts report with what their data shows, it aims to catch early warning signs before symptoms are noticeable.

NovaCare runs as standalone software on an onboard computer. After the first login it works without an internet connection, so the crew keeps access to health information and guidance even when Earth is out of reach.

What makes NovaCare different

A medical and psychological assistant in one. NovaCare answers physical health questions, such as headaches, vision changes or medication, and emotional ones, such as homesickness, anxiety or poor sleep. Each answer gives step-by-step guidance, says clearly when to escalate to the Crew Medical Officer or request a psychological conference, and cites its NASA source.

Instant risk response. Every new reading or answer is analyzed on board in seconds. NovaCare classifies each astronaut as Nominal, Watch, Needs attention or Critical, lists the most urgent crew members first, and when it detects signs of an emergency, such as chest pain, it tells the crew to act now and opens the emergency protocol, checking allergies and onboard supplies. No waiting for Earth.

Built for many environments. The same offline engine adapts to five mission profiles and can run on a low-cost computer anywhere on Earth. Only the knowledge base and reference settings change for each setting, and the interface is available in English, Spanish, Portuguese and French.

Problem On long missions, astronauts have limited access to medical knowledge, yet they are responsible for watching over their own health while doing demanding work.

Help from Earth is slow. From Mars, a message takes up to 20 minutes one way, so asking a question and getting an answer can take up to 40 minutes. In an emergency, that is too long.

The body changes fast. In microgravity, weight-bearing bones lose 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density per month on average. Muscle mass also drops faster than on Earth without the right diet and exercise. NASA's Human Research Program tracks both as official risks: bone fracture due to spaceflight-induced changes to bone, and reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness.

The mind is under pressure too. Isolation, confinement, distance from family and sleep loss affect mood and performance. NASA tracks these as risks of adverse cognitive or behavioral changes and of sleep loss and work overload.

Problems can stay hidden. Astronauts may report feeling fine while early signs of fatigue, stress, pain or illness are already showing in their data. The result is a real risk to the crew's health, their mission and their lives.

Objective NovaCare's objective is to become the onboard medical and psychological assistant that lets astronauts manage their physical and mental health autonomously during long-duration missions, when help from Earth is delayed or unavailable. It brings together tests, scanners, check-ins and self-reports into a single offline database for each astronaut. It learns each person's baseline and cross-checks what they report with what their data shows, to detect early warning signs before symptoms appear. It analyzes that information instantly, tells the crew how urgent each situation is, and turns it into personalized recommendations, guided sessions and emergency protocols based on NASA health standards, shifting space medicine from reactive to preventive.

Specific objectives

Create a personal baseline for each astronaut covering cardiovascular, respiratory, bone, muscle, immune, metabolic, psychological and sleep data.

Unify data from lab tests, daily check-ins and self-report surveys into one offline onboard database, designed to also accept wearables and onboard sensors.

Detect early warning signs by comparing each astronaut against their own baseline, not against a population average.

Cross-check what the crew reports with what their data shows, so hidden fatigue, stress or pain is flagged even when it goes unreported.

Classify every result instantly by urgency (Nominal, Watch, Needs attention or Critical) so the crew knows at once who needs help first.

Provide medical and psychological guided sessions, an offline question assistant and emergency protocols.

Keep each astronaut in control of their own health data, while critical information such as allergies and medication stays visible to the crew in an emergency.

Design for many environments from day one: different mission profiles in space and, on Earth, clinics, nursing homes, schools, workplaces, homes and remote sites.

Background NASA groups the risks of human spaceflight into five hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile, closed environments. Microgravity causes muscle loss, reduced bone density and cardiovascular changes. Radiation can damage cells and the immune system. Isolation and confinement can affect psychological well-being, which NASA's Human Research Program tracks as the risk of adverse cognitive or behavioral changes and psychiatric disorders.

Distance makes all of these harder to manage. Mars is on average 140 million miles (about 225 million km) from Earth, and a crewed mission would take roughly three years, compared with a three-day trip to the Moon. On the surface, astronauts would live in three-eighths of Earth's gravity for up to two years.

Space agencies have developed medical protocols and monitoring systems to reduce these risks, but they still rely heavily on support from the ground. Deep-space missions break that link. This is why autonomous health-monitoring software is essential.

Methodology We built NovaCare as a health-monitoring system that brings medical information from tests, check-ins and devices into one place. Development followed these stages:

Data model: defined the health data that matters in flight, from vital signs and exam results to sleep, mood and radiation exposure, and linked each indicator to the NASA Human Research Program risk it belongs to.

NASA evidence layer: queried NASA's OSDR Biological Data API and saved an offline snapshot of 646 datasets. We grouped the studies by body system and linked them to each of the 15 indicators NovaCare tracks.

Mission profiles: defined five environments (space station in low Earth orbit, deep-space transit, lunar base, Mars base and pressurized rover). Each one sets its own radiation dose, exercise target, communication delay with Earth and evacuation options, so guidance matches where the crew actually is.

Software development: designed and programmed a web application that works offline, with five sections: Home, My Health, Crew, Mission and Insights, available in English, Spanish, Portuguese and French.

Database integration: organized all information in a centralized medical record for each astronaut.

Baseline and instant analysis: compared each new result with the astronaut's own history the moment it is entered, classified it as Nominal, Watch, Needs attention or Critical, and calculated a daily readiness score.

Continuous monitoring: added one-minute daily check-ins, a 30-second mood check and a weekly mental health check that keep each record up to date.

Alerts, recommendations and emergency help: built notifications for concerning results, preventive recommendations, and a red Help button on every screen that alerts the whole crew and gives step-by-step instructions. Emergency instructions are available even without logging in.

Offline medical and psychological assistant: built a rule-based assistant, by text or voice, that answers from a knowledge base of 205 medical, wellbeing and habitat protocols referenced to NASA standards, and that recognizes emergencies and sends the crew straight to the emergency protocol.

Offline functionality: after the first login, the software works without a connection to Earth.

Prototype results The prototype is live at novacare.earth and delivers the core functions set out in our objectives.

Section | What the astronaut or crew can do Home | Start the daily one-minute check-in, log mood, ask questions, open the weekly mental health check (Mind), see today's readiness score and mission day My Health | Review heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, sleep, radiation dose and medical history, each marked Nominal, Watch, Needs attention or Critical and backed by the NASA OSDR studies behind it Crew | See each crew member's status and the allergies and medication needed in an emergency Mission | Switch mission profile, track mission status, active emergencies and low supplies Insights | See which crew members need attention first, shared risks such as high cabin CO₂, short sleep or a possible infection, and readiness trends over 14 days Help button (all screens) | Alert the whole crew and get step-by-step emergency instructions, even without logging in Questions assistant | Ask medical or emotional questions by text or voice, offline, with answers that cite their NASA source

Three examples from the working prototype:

Medical: when asked about a headache, the assistant considers space-specific causes such as high cabin CO₂ and fluid shifting toward the head. It gives step-by-step actions, explains when to alert the Crew Medical Officer, and cites NASA's risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and NASA-STD-3001.

Psychological: when an astronaut writes "I feel lonely and I miss my family," the assistant recognizes homesickness, suggests concrete steps such as scheduling a family call and sharing the feeling with the crew, says when to request a psychological conference, cites NASA's risk of adverse cognitive or behavioral changes, and offers to open Mind support.

Emergency: when an astronaut writes "I have chest pain," NovaCare responds at once that this sounds like an emergency, tells them to call the crew now, and opens the emergency protocol, checking the ship's inventory and the astronaut's allergies.

World impact In space, NovaCare improves crew safety and independence on long missions. It gives astronauts medical information, instant risk analysis and psychological support exactly when communication with Earth is limited. Because it adapts to each mission profile, the same system serves a space station today and a lunar or Mars base tomorrow.

On Earth, the same problem affects billions of people. The World Health Organization estimates that about 4.6 billion people lacked full coverage of essential health services in 2023, and 2.1 billion faced financial hardship from health costs in 2022. Isolation is a health problem on Earth too: 1 in 6 people worldwide is affected by loneliness, which WHO links to more than 871,000 deaths each year.

An offline system that tracks each person's baseline, notices changes early, tells people how urgent a situation is and gives clear medical and emotional guidance can help where a doctor is not always nearby:

Rural clinics with limited staff or unreliable internet

Nursing homes, where many people live with chronic conditions and some live in isolation

Schools and workplaces, for early detection and basic first response

Private homes, for older adults living alone

Remote and isolated sites, such as Antarctic research stations, ships, offshore platforms and disaster zones, which face the same isolation and distance from medical help that astronauts do

Adapting NovaCare to each of these settings does not require a new system: the same offline engine runs on a low-cost computer, and only the knowledge base, reference ranges and language change.
